# Draft:The Shadow of the Revolutionary Adrien Joseph Colson

Adrien Joseph Colson, a French lawyer and financial accountant to noble families before, during, and after the well know French revolution. His letters were featured in The Glory and The Sorrow book, written by Timothy Tackett. Colson left these letters to provide a window into how ordinary lawyer from the bourgeoisie experience’s the French Revolution. His letters reveal his journey as a lawyer in Paris and how Paris was before the start of the French Revolution. One of his known habits was writing these letters to his friend, Roch Lemaigre, who also happened to be a lawyer. Colson was also religiously connected to God, in which he often justifies things due religious purposes only. Adrien Joseph Colson born to a French family of nine siblings and two parents. All his eight siblings died either in infancy or in early childhood (Tackett, Ch 1, Pp. 10).Colson came to Paris from an exceedingly small town what were then the Austrian Lowlands in the northeast corner of France, located now in the state of Belgium. He was born in 1727 to live through until aftermath of French revolution in summer 1797. He was not a critic of King Louis XVI until king attempted to flee Paris. Overall, Colson was one of the French man's whose history is written for the future world to read.
Colson's career path before, during, and after the French Revolution. Colson, at the age of twenty-three, moved to Paris and started getting an education at the University of Reims to become an attorney a few years later. Colson earned a degree, “avocat en Parlement” (Tackett, Ch 1, Pp. 14) with the right to plead in the Parlement of Paris as a lawyer. Noted to be the most important court in France. Adrien Joseph Colson worked for noble families, like the Longaunay family and Burgundy wine company. He builds a great relationship with his employers and their sons, Alexandre-Maximilien- Francois and Antoine- Constantin, in which both are from the Marquis family. Furthermore, Adrien Joeseph Colson’s devoted his time toward his job only and worked for noble families.
Colson witnessed many of the French Revolution’s main events. Such as abolishing of Seigniorial system, creation of National Assembly, New Constitution, fall of Bastille, The Great Fear, Tennis Court Oath, attack on Bastille, lynching of the minister Foullon de Doue, Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen, and the Blessing of National Guard Flag, sermon of Abbe’ Claude Fauchet in 1789, attack on Tuileries Palace 1792, September massacres of 1792, execution of king Louis XVI in 1793, and finally the national guard of contingent of Lombards in 1793. Many of these events Colson had witnessed in person, but other events he heard about them from rumors in his neighborhood. Colson’s letters highlight three main points: French Revolution effect on Colson’s profession, Colson religious and political views, and Colson’s opinion regarding violence. Overall, Colson was always informed about the news and events happening in Paris. Many of the rumors may not be true, but overall, Colson would verify whatever is said to him by newspapers.
Colson’s letters show that many bourgeoisies initially hoped the French revolution would end with a constitutional monarchy. A system that is clear in every fair and just aspect. Colson, and many of those in his neighborhood, had never been a criticizer of King Louis XVI, not until 1792. After all the chaos that the lawyer had witnessed and all the rumors that he heard had pushed him into believing in the reality that the government was corrupt. Colson remained forgiven of the relentless actions from the kings until June 1791 (Tackett, Ch 7, Pp. 120). During that time, the king and his family attempted to flee Paris. Even after the king was captured and he signed off the New Constitution in September 1791, Colson and his neighbors remained Suspicious. Rumors about the king pulling out with these actions again were Surfacing. Furthermore, Colson was never a radical criticizer of the king, until the king's sneaky actions prevailed.
The French ordinary people, or the Third estate, became criticizing of King Louis XVI after the king attempt to flee Paris. Paris during that time in June 1791 was in a chaotic state. There was theft, massacre of the Champ de Mars, and more. When the king tried to flee the city with his family and leave the people without authority, the people felt betrayed. People no longer shouted, “long live the King” (Tackett, Ch 7, Pp. 122). There was a proposal to create a new regime that would replace the King and prevent his son from taking the throne. The people and Legislative Assembly were to create a constitutional monarchy that would give the people a chance to choose a newly organized “executive authority” (Tackett, Ch 7, Pp. 123). Meaning it called for a monarchy that does not include establishing a king. Preventing aristocrats from becoming dominant or better than ordinary citizens. Such as abolishing rights that are explicitly for the Second Estate, nobility. Such rights include collecting tolls and taxes from the Third Estate. Furthermore, people turned away from monarchy and ended their support for King Louis XVI because of lack of trust and responsibility. People no longer trusted the King, and the King could no longer stop massacres, which means he lacked responsibility.
Some of the changes brought by the French Revolution created complications for Colson, like ending of Seigneurial dues. Seigniorial dues and rights to collect tolls was exclusively for the nobility of the Second Estate in France. Seigniorial rights include the right to collect dues from peasants, run courts, charge tolls on roads and bridges, and compel locals to use their grain mills and baking ovens. They were first abolished, after the new revolutionary reforms in Paris (Tackett, Ch 7, pp. 101). Made Colson career exceedingly difficult to manage and even answer questions that were raised by his clients. Colson needed to settle things in the two major courts in Paris, the Parlement of Paris and the Chatelet was noted to be shut down and abolished leading to a new institution created. New laws were established or edited by deputies. For example, Colson had a job to pay seigniorial rights, and dues were supposed to be paid off over time but were abolished already (Tackett, Ch 7, Pp.102). There was no way for the lawyer to determine how much the family needed to pay in taxes or where he could settle it down. Furthermore, the unclear new system created few financial and responsibility burdens in how Colson needed to do his job.
Colson opposed many of the French Revolution’s religious reforms and it dechristianization efforts. Dechristianizers was an extremely sensitive and sad topic to Colson. Dechristianizers were a group of radical leftists who tried to de- Christianize the state of France. They had attempted in autumn of 1793 to abolish midnight mass on Christmas Eve, but they were met with mass of protesters. These masses let local national guards outside of the front door of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, so no city official tried to enter. The radical dechristianizers took control of the city because of the Terror policies. What Fueled the public more was the arrest of head priest of Colson’s parish and organist for no logical reason on September 12 (Tackett, Ch 9, Pp. 160). Bishops were pressured to resign, and most importantly the Cathedral of Notre Dame was converted into a Temple of Reason. Nuns were ordered to go home, including the streets name that contained religious names were to be changed. Most shocking was the order for all churches to be officially closed for religious practice (Tackett, Ch 9, Pp. 160) and confiscated objects. Colson was extremely sad about the dismantling of their local church. Colson was clearly against it but could do nothing. Furthermore, dechristinizers were successful in dechristinize the country. Indicating the religious tragedy that the lawyer witness shortly before his death.
Colson had also objected to the growing violence of the French Revolution and the Terror. He often opposed the violence of radicals, kings, and aristocrats. Colson called for the people to be fairly tried in courts without an indication of bloody scene to be displayed. But unfortunately, that was not followed, Colson often heard and even witnessed beheaded people on the streets, bodies lying dead on street, bloody fights, and more. Rumors about killings, fighting, arrests, and torture. Such scenes often make Colson upset and wrenched. Colson was notably against the six-deputies rule of executing king Louis XVI. January 21, 1793, was the king's execution day. He simply believed that the king should be imprisoned until his death (Tackett, Ch 8, pp. 141) and never released. Colson honestly believed in justice and peace, where people would not execute others. Another extreme case was the September Massacres of the year 1792. There was an invasion of the French kingdom by the Prussian army and the people feared that the army may release the prisoners. The people decided to go and kill everyone in the prisons including nobles, aristocrats, and criminals. Criminals had been serving their sentences for minor things, but they were killed out of fear. Colson condemned that mass killing as well. Furthermore, Colson was against violence of most forms and proposed that idea of trial in courts.
To review, Adrien Joseph Colson, a lawyer during the French Revolution, tells his story of what it is like living in the period of struggle and change. Even when the French revolution had a negative effect on his professional life, Colson stayed optimistic. He is an important historical figure because of his written letters that gives a new window into the French Revolution. His importance as a historical source comes from the documentation of historical French Revolution events that are not highlighted more in history. Overall, Colson was the man the history has forgotten.
References
Tackett, Timothy (2021). The Glory and The Sorrow: A Parisian and His World in the Age of the French Revolution. The Glory and the Sorrow: A Parisian and His World in the Age of the French Revolution - University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC)
